video_title: The AI Boom Is Bigger Than Anyone Thinks
gist: Dan Ives argues the AI build-out is under 15% complete ($4-5T capex, 13:1 Asian chip shortage until 2028-29) and is broadening to infrastructure, software, cybersecurity, Apple and energy, with regulation-driven slowdown calls seen as regulatory capture that benefits China. Pompliano pushes back that private frontier labs (Anthropic, OpenAI) face falling token prices and per-customer consumption as firms like his Silvia shift to sovereign, in-house models at ~97% lower cost.

insights.claim: Dan Ives says last quarter's hyperscaler monetization, specifically at Microsoft, was the inflection point for AI demand, and the trade is now spreading to second-, third- and fourth-derivative beneficiaries.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Look past first-order AI names toward derivative beneficiaries now that hyperscaler monetization is visible.
insights.quote: I think that was an inflection point quarter.

insights.claim: Ives estimates the AI spending cycle is less than 15% complete, with $4-5 trillion of spend over the next 3-4 years and a $5-6 multiplier across the rest of tech for every dollar of capex.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Implies a long runway for AI-linked revenue across tech beyond the direct capex recipients.
insights.quote: For every dollar of CapEx, there's a $5 to $6 multiplier across the rest of tech.

insights.claim: Ives says only about 4-5% of US companies have gone down the AI path, and he expects another 60-70% of enterprises globally (incl. Europe, Middle East, India) to adopt, which he calls bullish for hyperscalers.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Enterprise adoption is early; hyperscalers with installed bases capture the next adoption wave.
insights.quote: 4% of companies have gone down the AI path just in the US today.

insights.claim: Ives says the AI trade is broadening from memory to infrastructure names like Dell, HP and Cisco, and will next extend to energy and infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Rotate AI exposure into infrastructure, legacy hardware and energy rather than only chips/models.

insights.claim: Ives says AI chip supply-demand in Asia is running 13 to 1 and he does not expect chip equilibrium until late 2028 or early 2029.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A multi-year chip shortage supports semiconductor pricing power and earnings through 2028.
insights.quote: you don't have equilibrium till late 2028, early 2029 in terms of chips.

insights.claim: Ives argues the market is in the 'third inning' of the AI build-out and that even if 10-15% of data centers get voted down, a massive build-out will still occur over the next 12-18 months.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Local data-center opposition is a haircut, not a thesis breaker, in Ives's view.
insights.quote: even if 10 to 15% get voted down

insights.claim: Ives frames the AI cycle as a multi-year tech bull market and says investors still underestimate its scale, expecting two to three more years of massive growth.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Ives views pullbacks driven by narratives as buying opportunities.
insights.quote: we still have another two, three years of just massive growth.

themes.theme: Where to allocate in public AI

insights.claim: Ives's allocation framework: own the core winners (chips and hyperscalers Microsoft, Amazon, Google) and then position early in where the theme is heading, because once a transition is visible you have already missed it.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Core-plus-frontier positioning: anchor in chips/hyperscalers, add optionality ahead of transitions.
insights.quote: I just think you have to own chips. You got to own the hyperscalers

insights.claim: Ives argues Nvidia is cheaper today than 6-12 months ago despite investor fatigue, and that the full wave of physical AI is not yet reflected.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Nvidia fatigue may be mispriced relative to forward physical-AI demand.
insights.quote: You could argue that that stock is way cheaper today than it was 6 to 12 months ago

insights.claim: Ives says AMD under Lisa Su is 'just starting' on the AI chip side.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: AMD is a second chip beneficiary of the supply shortage.

insights.claim: Ives calls the 'SaaS apocalypse' a fictional narrative, citing Salesforce and ServiceNow, and says Palantir could become a category changer as its free cash flow ramps.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Software sold off on AI-disruption fears may be oversold.
insights.quote: The software, the SaaS apocalypse, I think it was a fictional narrative

insights.claim: Ives notes that in April the market declared cybersecurity 'done' because Anthropic would eat its lunch, yet CrowdStrike, Palo Alto and Zscaler have since recovered, illustrating overdone AI-disruption narratives.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Fade AI-disruption scares in incumbents with entrenched positions.
insights.quote: Cybersecurity is done. Anthropic's eating their lunch.

insights.claim: Ives says Apple's 1.5 billion iPhones and 2.5 billion iOS devices make it a 'toll collector on the consumer AI highway', and that bears missed this because the value is in the install base.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Distribution/install base, not model leadership, may capture consumer AI value.
insights.quote: You're now a toll collector on the consumer AI highway.

insights.claim: Ives says Meta was written off for heavy AI spending, but with 3.5 billion users it could afford to be late, and its stock has rebounded.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Massive user bases let incumbents catch up late in AI.
insights.quote: When you have 3 and 1/2 billion users, you could be late.

insights.claim: Ives says investors should watch Tesla's transition from EV maker to robotaxis, autonomy and Optimus, warning that once the transition happens it is already priced in.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Position before the physical-AI transition is visible in Tesla's numbers.
insights.quote: Once the transition happened, you've already missed it.

insights.claim: Ives argues consumer AI is a separate emerging investment category, that the consumer AI ad revolution is just starting, and that new stocks not discussed today will be prominent in 18-24 months.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Expect a new consumer-AI category of public names within two years.
insights.quote: we're just now starting the consumer ad revolution.

insights.claim: Ives says that if six months ago you had been told oil would be $105-110, the 10-year yield 5.2-5.3% and the Iran conflict ongoing, you would have guessed the S&P and Nasdaq about 15% lower than they are.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Market resilience against hostile macro signals an underlying growth driver.
insights.quote: You probably would be off by 15% lower.

insights.claim: Ives argues the elevated 10-year yield partly reflects AI-driven growth, increasing debt raises and data center capex rather than purely negative macro.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: High yields may be a symptom of the AI build-out, not just a headwind to it.
insights.quote: I could argue the 10-year is there because of the growth

insights.claim: Pompliano notes the macro backdrop looks negative (rising rates, ~$100 oil, 10-year above 5%, falling home prices, K-shaped economy) yet tech continues to lead.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Macro bears have a strong surface case that markets are currently ignoring.

insights.claim: Ives says weekend bear narratives tend to peak on Saturdays and are often reversed when leaders like Jensen Huang, Satya Nadella and Alex Karp speak, which he views as a buy-the-fear pattern.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Narrative-driven selloffs around AI-risk headlines tend to be buying opportunities.

themes.theme: Regulatory capture and the US-China race

insights.claim: Ives views calls from leading labs to slow AI as regulatory capture: Anthropic and OpenAI, leading the 'F1 race', want to throw sand in the gears so others cannot catch up.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Safety-driven regulation may entrench leaders; watch for policy that favors incumbents.
insights.quote: you go to the top floor and then you pull the ladder up.

insights.claim: Pompliano's framework: companies losing money and lacking non-dilutive capital call for an AI slowdown, while profitable ones like Meta and Google do not, so funding position determines which side of the regulatory debate a company takes.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Use cash-flow profile to predict a company's regulatory stance.

insights.claim: Ives argues the 'Dario essay' calling for caution added about 20% to Meta's stock as Zuckerberg chose to accelerate and gain share.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Competitors' caution can become share gains for aggressive incumbents.
insights.quote: I could argue like the Dario essay, that was 20% of that added to Meta's stock.

insights.claim: Ives says the AI race is a two-horse race between the US and China, that slowing down means China accelerates, and that every US data center shut down is a win for China.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Geopolitics argues against heavy US AI regulation, supporting continued capex.
insights.quote: every data center that gets shut down, China wins.

insights.claim: Ives says the White House meeting with Trump was needed to align the industry going into midterms because dystopian AI talk is fueling local opposition that shuts down data centers; he favors self-regulation over Beltway grandstanding.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Midterm politics are a near-term risk to data-center permitting.

insights.claim: Ives says the tech industry itself created the AI PR 'black eye' it is now contending with.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Industry messaging is a self-inflicted policy risk.

insights.claim: Ives names Jensen Huang and Alex Karp as the leaders who best understand AI, crediting Huang with the most global view and understanding that open source is needed for cost reasons, analogous to iPhone adoption depending on price.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Low token pricing and open models expand total demand, benefiting Nvidia.
insights.quote: Would you have 1.5 billion iPhones today? No.

insights.claim: Ives argues more jobs will be created by AI than destroyed over the next decade and that the job-loss narrative, like the SaaS apocalypse, is overdone.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Discount AI-unemployment narratives as policy and market risks.
insights.quote: More jobs will be created by AI than taken away over the next decade in my view.

themes.theme: Private labs' token economics and sovereign AI

insights.claim: Pompliano argues private frontier labs are in more trouble than people realize: since lab revenue equals token price times token consumption, and both price (price war) and per-customer consumption are falling, there is massive pressure on revenue.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of frontier-lab IPO valuations premised on per-customer usage growth.
insights.quote: It is token price times token consumption equals revenue.

insights.claim: Pompliano believes token consumption leads revenue and that revenue at large model labs, Anthropic in particular, has been plateauing because the general-intelligence approach is less valuable than expected.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Track token consumption as a leading indicator of lab revenue.
insights.quote: my belief is that token consumption leads revenue.

insights.claim: Pompliano says his company Silvia started as a ChatGPT wrapper, moved to Claude with compute spend rising to hundreds of thousands of dollars a month, then trained its own models and harness, shifting token consumption away from Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Fast-growing API customers may churn usage as they mature, a headwind for labs.
insights.quote: Our monthly compute expense went from zero to hundreds of thousands of dollars.

insights.claim: Pompliano says routing queries to Silvia's own models on its own hardware saves about 97% versus frontier models and also produces more accurate answers on tax, mortgage and credit card topics.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Applied, domain-specific models can beat frontier models on cost and accuracy.
insights.quote: the cost savings is about 97%.

insights.claim: Pompliano argues the key differentiator is applied versus general AI plus proprietary data, reinforcement learning and eval rubrics, so large enterprises with thousands of engineers will increasingly build their own.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Enterprise in-sourcing of AI is a structural headwind for model vendors and a tailwind for infrastructure.

insights.claim: Pompliano says a new low-cost model ('Jev') went from not existing three weeks ago to a $100 million run rate in its first week, and his engineers began routing queries to it where frontier models were cost prohibitive, describing fragmentation as 'death by 1,000 cuts' for frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Rapid model fragmentation erodes frontier-lab pricing power.

insights.claim: Ives agrees models will commoditize and says value in the chain will accrue to data, calling sovereign AI 'the golden goose' and the bigger debate than model players narrowing the gap.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Favor data owners and sovereign-AI enablers over pure model plays.
insights.quote: The models over time will become more commoditized.

insights.claim: Ives argues Anthropic and OpenAI have been smart in building enterprise sales forces, recognizing that monetization will come from enterprise rather than consumer.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Enterprise distribution is the labs' key moat against commoditization.

insights.claim: Ives says data is the new oil and gold, citing Amazon putting up gates against Muse, and Pompliano notes companies like MicroOne pay doctors and lawyers to create training data and that he was asked to license his podcast for data.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Proprietary data is becoming a monetizable asset class.
insights.quote: Data is the new oil and gold.

themes.theme: AI IPOs and the IVAI fund

insights.claim: Ives says he would be shocked if Anthropic does not IPO before year-end (later suggesting after the midterms), and argues Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX going public would be good for the overall tech trade.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Mega private-AI IPOs could be a near-term catalyst for the sector.
insights.quote: I'd be shocked if that doesn't happen.

insights.claim: Pompliano cautions that a good product does not equal a good company, pointing to S-1 data points and trends suggesting more headwinds for the AI labs than investors assume.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Separate product enthusiasm from unit economics when evaluating AI IPOs.
insights.quote: a good product does not equal a good company.

insights.claim: Ives has launched the Ives Ultra Fund (ticker IVAI), a $200 million publicly traded permanent-capital vehicle that he describes as the first public company to invest in private AI tech companies.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Offers public-market access to private AI names; note it is the guest's own product.
